en: [1] [Success! Homage to Śrī Cakrasaṃvara!
Victorious in this world is that very Lord of the Mind, embraced by the arms of the beloved of the world, whose heart is perpetually blissful;
by him was this form manifested for the sake of the welfare of the universe.
The unreal is more distorted; the real is the innermost nature.

Regarding the objection as to why there is no introductory statement (nidānavākya) beginning with "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*) at the very start of this tantra, some masters explain that because the Blessed One is eternal, his final nirvāṇa (*parinirvāṇa*) is simply not possible. And it has been said:

"The Buddha does not pass into final nirvāṇa. Furthermore, if final nirvāṇa were possible, the compilers of the collection would have to state an introductory statement; for instance, such is the case in the Sūtra.

"Monks, after I have passed into parinirvāṇa, my Dharma is to be compiled beginning with the words 'Thus have I heard' (*evam mayā śrutam*). Others, however, say that this tantra has been extracted from other tantras without the introductory formula (*nidānavākya*). First of all, since discerning people engage [with a work] only after perceiving the relationship between the expression and the expressed, as well as the purpose and the purpose of the purpose, those very things are now set forth. As it has been said: "A listener proceeds to listen only when the subject matter is established and the relationship is established."
Therefore, at the beginning of a treatise, the connection together with its purpose must be stated.

In this context, first of all, the entire textual composition known as the *Saṃcāra*, beginning with the words "atha ataḥ," constitutes the expression (*abhidhāna*). That which is expressed by it—the nature of the Lord (*bhagavat*) and the Goddess (*bhagavatī*)—is the subject matter (*abhidheya*). The relationship between these two is characterized as that of expression and expressed. Others maintain that the relationship is characterized as that of means and end (*upāyopeyabhāva*). Furthermore, the purpose (*prayojana*) is the diligent, uninterrupted, and long-term practice of the meaning of the *Saṃcāra*; and the attainment of the state of the glorious *Saṃvara* is the ultimate purpose of the purpose (*prayojanaprayojana*).

Now, regarding the phrase "atha ata" and so forth: in this collection of indeclinables (*nipātasamudāya*), the word *atha* signifies immediate succession (*ānantarya*), and the word *ataḥ* signifies sequence (*krama*). The meaning is: immediately following the *Khasama-tantra*, according to the sequence that will be explained by this [text]. "I shall fully proclaim" (*saṃpravakṣyāmi*) means I shall speak correctly and without error. "The procedure for movement" (*saṃcāravidhi*)—movement (*saṃcāra*) refers to the roaming of the yoginīs within the body of the yogin and within the maṇḍala; its "procedure" (*vidhi*) is its method, its arrangement, its regulation. "Supreme" (*uttama*) means...

It is "supreme" because it serves as the cause for attaining the unsurpassed state. "Tāraya" (save) means "tāraṇam" (saving), which here signifies "plāvana" (flooding or immersing). Therefore, "tāraya" means "make them flood [with realization]," that is to say, "reveal it to sentient beings. The word "Vajrapāṇe" (O Vajrapāṇi) is understood as the vocative address; for this very reason, Vajrapāṇi is the compiler (*saṃgītikṛt*). "Idam" (this) refers to this procedure for the movement [of consciousness] held in the mind. Of what nature is it? It is "established in the path of the yoga of the self of the three wheels. The Blessed One is the "self of the three wheels"; his "yoga" is the meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

That very [path], because it brings about the goal in successive stages, is the *mārga* (path). It is established in that form. Again, asking what kind it is, he says: "concealed," and so forth. "Concealed" means not made manifest among those who lack faith. "Yat" means which. "Tathā" means even so; the meaning is: even though it possesses the nature of a path. "In the *tantra*" means in the *Lakṣābhidhāna*. How is it concealed? He says: "arranged in direct and reverse order."

The meaning is that its concealment results from being expressed through both sequential order and transposition of order. To show that the enumeration (*uddeśa*) and so forth were taught therein by means of sequential order and transposition, he says: "The enumeration," and so on. It is called *uddeśa* because it is enumerated; it is the aphorism (*sūtra*). "As it was spoken" means as it was correctly stated. It is called *nirdeśa* because it is explained exhaustively; it is the nature of the commentary (*vṛtti*). It is called *pratinirdeśa* because it is explained in relation to the unmanifest *nirdeśa*; it is the sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*). "All indeed"—this refers to the totality.

These three constitute the "extensive procedure for the ritual of the convention" (*saṃketavidhivistara*); the meaning is that it is more extensive by means of the ritual of the convention. To the question, "What is its power?", he says, "By which," and so forth. "By which" refers to the procedure of movement. "Merely by being known" means: merely by being specifically known through the power of cultivation (*bhāvanā*) and gradually brought into direct realization (*sākṣātkārīkṛta*). The practitioner (*sādhaka*), whose nature is the vow (*saṃvara*), "shall attain"—that is, obtain—"accomplishment" (*siddhi*), which is Buddhahood. Now, in order to demonstrate the meaning of the tantra, he says, "Seven," and so forth.

"By means of the thirty-seven yogas" means by way of the connection with the thirty-seven deities together with the Blessed One. "Factors of enlightenment" refers to the qualities conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), such as the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and so forth. "Renowned and manifested in the world" means that, because they are of the nature of skillful means (*upāya*), they have attained fame through being manifested in the world. To the question, "In what way do these possess the nature of skillful means? he says: "The supreme [deity] Śrī Heruka of the world. The mention of "Śrī Heruka" is an illustration; it should be understood that Pracaṇḍā and the others are also included.

Because these—Śrī Heruka and the others—are the primary factors in the world when cultivated as the factors conducive to awakening (bodhipākṣika), such as the applications of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna); therefore, they constitute the "means" (upāya). This is the intended meaning. Now, in order to show the sequence of cultivation (bhāvanākrama), he says: "First," and so forth. "First" means at the commencement of cultivation. "By the Lord of Yoga" means that through resolute conviction (adhimokṣa), one instantly possesses the yoga of Śrī Saṃvara. "The ego-identification with the five aggregates" means the identification of oneself as the deity within the five aggregates.

The section beginning with "the aggregate of form" (*rūpaskandha*) is easy to understand. Regarding "the elements" (*dhātu*), the elements (*dhātavaḥ*) are also described in the form of deities. The section beginning with "the earth element" (*pṛthivīdhātu*) is self-evident. The conclusion is given by the words beginning with "thus" (*evam*). This is the first exposition. || 1 ||

"Then," and so forth. One should connect [the text] as follows: "Which are all those factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharma) that are to be joined through the yoga of the deities? "The production of supernatural power" (ṛddhyutpāda) means that by means of this, supernatural power is produced. "The production of supernatural power through desire" (chandarddhyutpāda) means that desire itself is the production of supernatural power. The others are to be understood in the same way. The conclusion is given with the words "these," and so forth. This is the second exposition. || 2 ||

Regarding the passage beginning with "tatraiteṣām" (there, of these), all of this demonstrates that the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and so forth have the nature of deities. The remainder is easy to understand. Thus ends the third exposition. || 3 ||

Now, regarding the passage beginning with *athāta* and so forth: "non-duality with the heroes" (*vīrādvayam*) means the non-dual unity of the yogin, whose essence is the venerable Saṃvara, with the heroes such as Khaṇḍakapāla and others. To the question "In what way is there non-duality?", he says: "The venerable Heruka," and so forth. "*Aṅgāṅga*" is the brief statement (*uddeśa*). "*Sarvāṅgāvayava*" is the detailed explanation (*nirdeśa*). "*Nakhadantayoḥ*" and so forth is the specific application (*pratinirdeśa*). Thus ends the fourth explanation. 4.

The passage beginning with "Then, another" (*athānyatamam*) and so forth is easy to understand. Regarding "the internal [maṇḍala] as it is" (*ādhyātmikaṃ yathā*) and so forth: the connection is that the external maṇḍala is to be known just as the internal one is. "How the placement (*nyāsa*) is to be applied" means that just as the placement of the deities is to be explained immediately hereafter, so too should that [external placement] be understood. Now, in order to introduce the placement of the deities, he says "on the support" (*ādhāra*) and so forth.

The meaning is that one should contemplate the wheel, which consists of the nature of the support and the supported, as situated above the wind-mandala and so forth, which have been transformed from the syllable *yaṃ* and others. Regarding the phrase "having known" and so on: having visualized these four mandalas, "whatever other rite there may be"—this refers to another ritual procedure. "This, in due order according to the lineage of gurus"—the remainder is that this very procedure taught by the guru is to be visualized in its proper sequence. Regarding the verse beginning with "on the mountain" and so forth:

The meaning is as follows: upon the summit of Mount Sumeru, which has arisen from the transformation of the syllable *sūṃ*, situated above the four mandalas of wind and so forth just mentioned, there is the pericarp of a multicolored eight-petaled lotus, which has arisen from the transformation of the syllable *paṃ*. "The Hero (Vīra) stands there in the center" means that he stands there upon the pericarp. From the syllable *hūṃ* produced from the space-locus situated within the moon-mandala, which has arisen from the transformation of the vowels (*āli*) and consonants (*kāli*), Vīreśvara—having transformed [into his form] and having stepped forward in the *ālīḍha* posture, treading upon Gaurī and her lord—stands upon the sun-mandala; this is the intended sense. "Ḍākinī," and so forth.

By this verse, the placement (*nyāsa*) of Ḍākinī and the others in the petals of the eastern and other directions in counter-clockwise order is described. "Two-armed and one-faced" means that all of these are two-armed and possess one face. "Sporting in various forms" means that they possess diverse forms and are playful. The passage beginning with "in the intermediate directions" and so forth is easy to understand. "Having joined the syllable *pu* and so forth" means having mentally superimposed Pullīramalaya and the other locations.

"Established in each land" means established in those places such as Pullīramalaya and so forth, together with [the goddesses] Pracaṇḍā and the rest, [namely] Khaṇḍakapālī and the others. "Having brought" means having brought them. "Situated within the center of the wheel" means having placed them in the middle of the three wheels, beginning with the *cittacakra*. "One should worship" means one should meditate upon them. "Always" means at every junction (*saṃdhyā*). Regarding "pu" and so forth: "pu" is the brief designation (*uddeśa*); "Pullīramalaya" is the detailed explanation (*nirdeśa*). This applies everywhere. Everything is easy to understand. "In the mouth" means in the cardinal directions, the faces of the quarters.

"Vimukha" means in the intermediate directions. "Thus," and so forth: "thus" refers to the mandala as previously described. "External and internal" means both the exterior and the interior. "Having taken as an object" means one should take it as an object. As for how long [one should do so], he says: "as far as the sphere of cessation. This means as long as nirvāṇa has not become the object. Thus ends the fifth instruction. (5)

"Then," and so forth. "Of the host of mudrās characterized by universal sovereignty and the like" means that the Blessed One is the sovereign of all deities; by the word "and the like" (*ādi*), Vajravārāhī and others are included. The connection with what follows is: "the determination of the collection of mudrās consisting of the essential forms of their symbols. The word "I shall speak" (*vakṣye*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. "Their own color, arms, and posture" refers to the respective colors and other attributes of the deities. "In the secret tantra" (*gopyatantra*) means that having been concealed in the extensive tantra, I shall speak of them here; such is the intention.

“Śrīheruka,” and so forth, is easy to understand. “Embracing with both hands” means that he holds a vajra and a vajra-bell with his two embracing arms; this is the ellipsis. “The right [hand] raised” means that these are the symbols on the raised right arms. “Skull and blood” means a skull-cup filled with blood. “A severed head” means a raised head of Brahmā. “The left [hand]” is as before, referring to the symbols on the raised left arms. Thus it is explained.

"Adorned with twenty-four half-[units]" means that one should meditate upon the Blessed One as he is renowned to be adorned with twelve arms by virtue of bearing twelve symbols. "A hundred and a half, however, should be known as a garland of heads" means that he wears a garland of fifty severed heads. "The sacrificial [thread]" means that he wears the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*). "He should be placed in the presence of the Blessed Lady" implies that one should see the Blessed Lady standing before him.

"And [she who holds] a skull-cup in her embrace, bearing the blood of the wicked Māras"—this means she holds with her left embracing arm a skull-cup filled with the blood and entrails of the wicked. "Always holding a threatening gesture and a vajra against the wicked"—this means she always holds with her right arm a vajra accompanied by a threatening forefinger (*tarjanī*). "[She whose] girdle is adorned with fragments"—this means her waist region is adorned with a girdle made of broken pieces.

"Non-dual through the union of both" means that the forms of the Blessed Lord and the Blessed Lady have entered into meditative absorption (*samāpatti*). "But the Ḍākinīs and so forth" refers to the Ḍākinīs and the rest. "Four" means four [female deities]. "With a skull-topped staff and a skull-cup" means that all of them hold a skull-cup together with a *khaṭvāṅga* in their left hands. "A small knife" means they hold a flaying knife (*kartikā*) in their right hands. "Of the body adorned with the five mudrās and so forth" means that they wear the five mudrās upon their bodies as appropriate; by the word "and so forth," armlets and other ornaments are included.

“Resplendent with loose hair” means shining with loose locks of hair. “With twenty-four heroes” means there are twenty-four heroes. “Adorned with the five mudrās and so forth” means they wear the five mudrās, such as the necklace (*kaṇṭhikā*) and others. By the word “and so forth,” anklets, armlets, and the like are included. “Two-armed and one-faced” means they have two arms and one face. “The turban marked by the matted-hair crown” uses the nominative plural.

"Embracing through the passioning of one's own symbol with great passion (*mahārāga*)" means that great passion (*mahārāga*) is innate bliss (*sahajānanda*). "Passioning" is the act of being impassioned for the sake of that [bliss]; thus, the sense is that they hold the vajra and vajra-bell with two arms engaged in embracing for that reason. "Wearing the five mudrās and so forth as crest-jewels"—by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), armlets and other ornaments are included; the meaning is that they wear the five mudrās and so forth together with a crest-jewel. "Adorned with a girdle" means their waist regions are decorated with a girdle.

"Grasping the yoga-vessel" means holding a skull-cup (*kapāla*) with the left hand. "Beginning with Śrī Heruka" refers to Śrī Heruka and the others. "All" means every one of them. "Endowed with the *ālīḍha* posture" is in the nominative plural. He states the specific attributes of Śrī Heruka with the words beginning with "necklace" (*kaṇṭhikā*). Regarding the phrase "the six are proclaimed as the mudrās: the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), ashes (*bhasma*), and the [five] seals," the meaning is that according to this sequence, the six seals beginning with the necklace, together with the sacred thread and ashes, are proclaimed.

"Adorned with the six seals by virtue of the purity of the six perfections" means that the Blessed One’s body is adorned with the six seals purified by the six perfections; this is the intended meaning. "By way of the nature of the three syllables through the division of body, speech, and mind" refers to the three syllables which, having the nature of body and so forth, have attained the form of sound (*nāda*). The nature that arises from those [syllables] in the form of the syllable *HŪṂ* is the "nature of the three syllables. From that, one must supply the word "arisen."

"One should meditate on oneself as the essential nature" means that one should meditate on oneself through the essential nature of Śrī Saṃvara. "What need is there for others for those desiring accomplishment?"—this is a statement of majesty explaining that for a yogin who aspires to Buddhahood, what purpose is served by other alternative natures? He states the benefit with the words beginning "Whatever merit... and so forth. "It comes to be" (bhavate) means "it arises. "Of him" refers to the practitioner of the Saṃvara yoga. "Many-faced" is the brief indication; "thousand-faced" is the detailed explanation.

"Even with a thousand mouths"—this is the meaning. "Of that merit" means *tat-puṇya*. "The practitioner" means *sādhakasya*. "The expansion of qualities" means extensive qualities (*vistīrṇa-guṇa*). "Kākāsyā and the others, four" means the four beginning with Kākāsyā. "All the gates are blocked" means all these [deities] remain having obstructed the four gates. "Yamadāḍhī" refers to the four beginning with Yamadāḍhī. "Four in the corners" means in the four corners.

"Likewise, with one foot" means with the *ālīḍha* stance. "For two forms are captivating" means that each of the four goddesses, Yamadāḍhī and the others, possesses two captivating forms. "Just as for the host of Ḍākinīs" implies "just as the colors of Ḍākinī and the others. "But Kākāsyā and the others according to their divisions" means they abide in unmixed forms according to the specific divisions of Kākāsyā and the rest. The conclusion is given by the words beginning with "In this way."

"Abiding in the entire wheel" means [abiding] in all those situated in the wheel. "The sequence of the method for the differentiation of syllables" is used in the sense of the first case (nominative). This is an elliptical indication; it should be understood that the arms and so forth are also included. Thus ends the sixth instruction. 6.

Now, regarding the passage beginning with "I shall speak of the two armors" (*atha kavacadvayaṃ vakṣye*): "The two armors" refers to the pair of hexads of armor-mantras belonging to the Lord and the Goddess. To the question "Having done what?", he says: "The determination in the secret tantras. This means that having concealed within the extensive tantras the determination—the certainty—of that pair of hexads, by which its certainty is established, I shall explain it clearly here in this tantra. "With *astra*" means it is joined to all the limbs according to the convention of the Dharma.

The intention is that the application of *oṃ ha* and so forth should be performed at the heart and other locations. First, regarding "Vajrasattva indeed": Vajrasattva is to be visualized in the heart either as being actually present or through resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*). In this same manner, Vairocana and the others, as well as Vajravārāhī and the others, are to be understood as being described immediately thereafter. And "the weapon alone" refers to all the limbs. "The Yoginī of non-dual heroism" means that her yoga is the meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) for the sake of non-dual gnosis with the Hero; she who possesses this is the "Yoginī of non-dual heroism"—this is the meaning. Thus ends the seventh instruction. (7)

"Then," and so forth. "By means of the two armors" refers to those mentioned immediately above. "The self" refers to one's own body, which consists of the essence of Śrī Saṃvara; the ellipsis is that one should armor it according to its respective places. "The wisdom-wheel has been visualized" means that one should visualize the wisdom-maṇḍala, brought forth by the rays from the seed-syllable in the heart, in front of oneself. "Having caused [them] to enter" means one should cause them to enter. "Swiftly" means without [offering] water for honor (*argha*), water for the feet (*pādya*), and so forth. "By means of the mudrā and mantra" refers to the two mudrās and mantras to be described below. "The yogin" refers to the practitioner. "With feet stepped upon" [refers to the following].

"Having stepped upon the right foot with the left foot," "with an upward gaze" means with a gaze turned upward and to the left; "with the head" means with the face; "by the sound of the syllable *pheṃ*" means by the utterance of the *pheṃ* mantra. "The world-systems of the ten directions shall be drawn forth by the heroes and yoginīs" means that by this mantra, the heroes and yoginīs residing in the world-systems of the ten directions are summoned. "But the incitement is by the mantra" means that one should incite the wheel of gnosis (*jñānacakra*) by means of this very mantra.

"One should summon" means one should attract [the deity] instantly by means of the mudrā that will be described; "jhaṭiti" (instantly) is the meaning. Regarding "having made," etc.: "that" refers to the mudrā. "In the middle of the forehead" means in the center of the forehead. "By revolving in a whirlpool-like fashion" means one should rotate it again and again. Now, in order to show the meditative union (*samāpatti*), he says: "one should empower," etc. "One should empower" means that preceded by the recitation of the mantra, one should cause [the deities] to kiss one another in their respective places. "The Yoginī and the Hero" refers to the Goddess and the God.

"Non-dual" (*advaya*) refers to the sign of meditative attainment (*samāpatti-nimitta*). "At the tip of the nose" means on the lotus of the nose. "On the excellent *varaṭaka* of the *liṅga*" means on the *varaṭaka* of the *vajra*. "One should empower together with the host of mantras" means that, preceded by the recitation of the heart and subsidiary heart mantras of the Blessed Lord and the Blessed Lady, the Blessed Lord should kiss the Blessed Lady at the navel and other locations; such is the meaning. "The Yoginī Buddha-Ḍākinī" refers to Vajravārāhī. "On the tongue" means on the tongue.

"By means of the two *avadhūtas*" refers to the two mantras of the Heart and the *Upahṛdaya* of the Blessed One. "One should empower the Hero" means that one should kiss the Blessed One, the Hero, starting from the navel. "The non-duality of the Yoginī and the Hero" means that having performed all this, one should meditate upon the Hero as being in union with the Yoginī; this is the meaning. He states the purpose of this union with the words beginning with "bliss" (*ānanda*). "The Hero" means like a hero; "the Yoginī" means like a yoginī.

The intended meaning is that these two possess the nature of wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*) with respect to the bliss of sexual union (*suratānanda*). The phrase "all indeed" (*samastaṃ vai*) means that all three [of them] are likewise so. He states this very point with the words beginning with "that" (*tad*). "That bliss" (*tatsukha*) refers to the bliss accompanied by sexual union. "Means" (*upāya*) refers to the activity characterized by movement. "The All-Knowing One" (*sarvavid*) refers to the conventional bodhicitta, which is of the nature of the *saṃbhogakāya*. The meaning is that all three, by virtue of their commonality with the innate (*sahaja*), have the innate bliss (*sahajānanda*) as their essential nature. He speaks of the majesty of the innate bliss:

By the words beginning with *martya* [it is meant]: "one form" (*ekamūrtim*) means a single nature. "In an instant" (*kṣaṇāt*) means from innate bliss (*sahajānanda*). The meaning is that by the power of innate bliss, mortals and the rest become of the nature of great bliss (*mahāsukha*). As for "meditation has indeed been taught by me," the meditation on the drawing-in of the wheel of gnosis (*jñānacakra*) by means of the mudrā and mantra has already been taught. Regarding "the withdrawal" (*saṃhāra*), it is the entry of the drawn-in wheel of gnosis into one's own self. "Recalled as the ritual" (*vidhismṛtam*) means as it was explained at length in the extensive tantra according to the prescribed rule.

The ellipsis is that "this is now being explained. He demonstrates the withdrawal itself with the words beginning with "vāmā" and so forth. "Whirling" means by means of the rotation. "The ḍākinīs [attain] that bliss" means that through that mudrā, the satisfaction of the yoginīs arises. The sense is that, preceded by the recitation of the mantra "Oṃ, all phenomena are pure through yoga; I am pure through yoga," one should cause the gnosis-maṇḍala to enter the commitment-maṇḍala by means of this mudrā. Thus ends the eighth instruction. || 8 ||

"Then," and so forth. "The emanation body" (*nairmāṇika*) refers to the deity's body, which has the nature of an emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), consisting of the manifestation and withdrawal [of forms] for the sake of the world; this is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. "That which is to be known, the enjoyment body—listen to it from here": the connection is that one should listen to the enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*) which is to be known by means of this sequence about to be explained. "The Mahāyāna" means that by which they go is a vehicle (*yāna*); it is both great and a vehicle, hence "Mahāyāna. "Mahāmudrā" is the body of the glorious *Saṃvara*.

"Thus [he] grants the accomplishments (*siddhi*) of the yoginīs"—that is to say, in such a manner, by means of teaching the Dharma to the yoginīs and others who reside within the peaked pavilion (*kūṭāgāra*), he bestows accomplishment; this is the meaning. For this very reason, because he is enjoyed by the deities residing in the peaked pavilion through the gateway of the enjoyment of the Dharma, he is called the *saṃbhogakāya*. Regarding "there is nothing superior to Mahāmudrā": there exists no other excellence. Why? He says:

"Supreme among all yogas" means that because this is the most excellent yoga among all yogas, for that reason; what, then, is this? He says: "The glorious Heruka, the Great King, the Lord of all yogas, the Sovereign. All of this is easy to understand. In every instance, the accusative case is used in the sense of the nominative. "Extracted from the Equal to Space" means that precisely because of its excellence, it has been extracted from the tantra named *Khasama*. "Consisting of the wisdom of the Omniscient One" means that its nature is that wisdom called Great Bliss (*mahāsukha*) which belongs to the Omniscient Ones, the Perfectly Awakened Buddhas.

By this easily understood verse beginning with "Śrī Heruka, the supreme hero," the communal feast (*gaṇabhojana*) in the center is indicated. This is for the purpose of explaining that by means of this very yoga, together with fellow practitioners of equal intent, one should accomplish both mundane and supramundane attainments (*siddhi*) through the ritual procedures such as the drinking of *soma* and so forth. "Having joined the syllable *pu* and so on" means having mentally projected (*āropya*) Pullīramalaya and the other sites. "Established in each region" refers to the host of deities such as Pracaṇḍā and others who are established in those respective regions.

"Having become the self of Śrī Heruka"—one must supply the words "one should meditate upon the self of Śrī Heruka. To the question "How should one meditate?", he says: "having placed the twenty-four syllables. The meaning is that having placed the twenty-four syllables beginning with *pu* on the head and other parts [of the body], one should meditate upon the channels (*nāḍī*) located therein as being in the form of Pracaṇḍā and the others. Concluding, he says: "the Enjoyment Body," and so forth. By this sequence, "the Enjoyment Body" (*sāṃbhogika*) refers to the *saṃbhogakāya*.

"Renowned" (*khyātam*) means "described. "Established in the great yoga" (*mahāyogavyavasthitam*) means established by taking the *mahāyoga* samādhi as the standard; such is the meaning. Regarding "but the process" (*pravṛttiṃ tu*), one should understand that by this sequence one should know the arising of Śrī Heruka. Regarding "but the cessation is described as previously indicated" (*nivṛttiṃ tu yathoddiṣṭaṃ kathyate*), the meaning is that his cessation—that is, his negation—through the meditation on the *dharmakāya*, which was previously mentioned, is now being described. The passage beginning with "the syllable Śrī" (*śrīkāram*) and so forth is easy to understand.

"These are empty by their own nature" means that these—the arms, faces, and so forth—are empty of the forms of apprehended object and apprehending subject by their own nature; they are devoid of intrinsic nature because, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), their nature is great bliss (*mahāsukha*). And that great bliss is "all-pervading," meaning it permeates the entire world. It is "unstruck" (*anāhata*) in the sense that it is unimpeded by conceptual constructions such as the apprehended object and so forth. The phrase beginning with "having meditated" (*bhāvayitvā*) and so forth is easy to understand.

"But the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment will certainly arise there"—this means that those thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment which exist will arise through cultivation therein. Thus ends the ninth exposition. (9)

"Then," and so forth. "Wearied by meditation, one should withdraw" means that when one is weary of meditation and wishes to rise, one should withdraw the deities of the maṇḍala within oneself and then arise. Having arisen, what should be done? He says: "By the specific form of conduct," and so forth. "By the specific form of conduct" refers to the conduct during the state of non-composure (*asamāhita-caryā*). "The union and separation of yoga" refers to the abandonment of the pride of being Śrī Saṃvara. "Of these" refers to this [conduct]. "Of those practicing conduct" refers to one who is engaged in the conduct of non-composure.

Now, he speaks in order to explain the performance of the *bali* offering, beginning with the words "properly" (*yathāvat*) and so forth. "Properly" means without error. Having meditated upon what was previously mentioned—meaning having visualized before oneself the previously described *cakra* brought forth by means of the mudrā and mantra—"according to the rite" (*vidhi*) means by means of the rite of the vajra-añjali. "In detail" (*vistara*) means consisting of an abundance of liquor, meat, and so forth. "Should be given" (*dātavyam*) means it is worthy of being offered, having been prepared according to the rite of tasting the nectar (*amṛta*). "In the rites" (*karmasu*) refers to for the sake of rites such as pacification (*śāntika*) and others.

"Specifically" (*viśeṣataḥ*) means by means of a particular manner of rotating with the left and right [hands]. "The dark fortnight" (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*) and so forth is easy to understand. He states the procedure for summoning the circle of those to be fed (*bhojayitavyacakrākarṣaṇavidhi*) with the words beginning with "stepped upon" (*ākrānta*); this has already been explained previously. To clarify this very point, he says "the previously mentioned mudrā" (*pūrvoktamudrā*) and so forth. "The previously mentioned mudrā" refers to the *jvālāmudrā*. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the upward gaze preceded by the treading of the feet is indicated. "Mantra" (*mantra*) refers to the syllable *pheṃ*.

"By means of yogas" means by the application (*yojana*) of these [elements], such as the mudrās; "having brought forth the maṇḍala" is the ellipsis. "Having protected" means having protected according to the prescribed rule; that is to say, having visualized oneself in the form of Śrī Saṃvara according to the ritual procedure, and having armored oneself with the two armors (*kavaca*). He states the mantra: *oṃ* and so forth. "Thus" refers to this mantra. It is connected with what follows: "well-established and consecrated with the sacramental substances (*samayadravya*) and so forth. The sacramental substances are the *gokudahanā* (cow-flesh) and so on.

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), one should understand rice, condiments, and so forth. "Well-placed" (*susthitam*) means having been properly prepared and set down according to the procedure for tasting the nectar (*amṛta*). "With the upward-blossoming" (*ūrdhvavikacayā*) refers to the upward-blossoming [gesture]. Regarding "to the heroes and yoginīs" (*vīrayoginī*): the ellipsis is that one should offer it to the hero together with his consort, and to the yoginīs beginning with Ḍākinī and ending with Yamamathanī. Furthermore, to the heroes such as Khaṇḍakapāla and others, one should offer it by reciting once the mantra beginning with *oṃ kara kara*, namely: *oṃ kha kha khāhi khāhī*, and so forth.

The meaning is that [the offering] should be given to the guardians of the directions by reciting this mantra twice. To show that one should offer the *bali* while joined with the yoga of the deity, he says "Vīra," and so forth. "Vīra" refers to the Blessed Lord. He alone is the *mantra* because of his contemplation of reality (*tattva*) and because he protects the world. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), there is an inclusion of all deities such as Vajravārāhī. Their "circle" (*cakra*) is the peaked pavilion (*kūṭāgāra*). "Adorned with cremation grounds and so forth" means it is endowed with the eight cremation grounds and other features.

By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the outer vajra-fence (*vajrāvalī*) is to be understood. "Facing south" is intended as an illustration; by this, it should be understood that one is naked and has disheveled hair. "In high places" means seated upon a corpse in a high location such as a cremation ground or a mountain. "Worshipped" means one should meditate [upon the deity]. Having meditated, what should be done? To this he says: "It should be given," and so forth. "It should be given" refers to liquid substances and the like; one should offer these to the deities.

"By one's own power" means according to one's capacity, in accordance with one's wealth; this is the sense. "Characterized by the proper sequence" means that the consecration (*saṃskāra*) has been cultivated without transgressing the sequence of meditative visualization (*pratibhāvanā*). Now he speaks of the communal feast (*gaṇabhojana*) with the words beginning with "under Puṣya. Regarding "having performed worship": having performed the five-fold worship (*pañcopacāra-pūjā*) for the sake of the Yoginīs. "All that exists should be given" means that everything available—food, condiments, and so forth—should be prepared. "The assembly of all virtuous people" refers to the *gaṇamaṇḍala*.

"Therein" means in the maṇḍala of the gaṇas. "The entirety contained in two vessels" refers to all the food, condiments, and so forth, together with the liquid substances, as they reside within the two vessels. "Consecrated" means accomplished through the procedure for the tasting of nectar (*amṛta*). He states the benefit [of this] with the words beginning with "of that," etc. "Of the excellent ones" means the excellent things. Thus ends the tenth instruction. || 10 ||

"Then," and so forth. "The six *pāramitās* and so on" refers to the six beads beginning with the necklace (*kaṇṭhikā*). "And so on" (*ādi*) means the primordial accomplishments (*ādisiddhas*). "The *pāramitās*" means that they have the nature of the *pāramitās*; this is the meaning. Regarding "enlightenment" (*bodhi*) and so forth: the phrase "and indeed the thirty-sixth enlightenment" is to be connected with the words "the essence of the deity of supreme longevity. "Supreme longevity" (*paramāyuḥ*) refers to right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*).

The meaning of "consisting of deities" is that the bodies of deities such as Śrī Heruka and others, together with perfect meditative absorption (*samyaksamādhi*), have the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipākṣika*) as their intrinsic nature. Regarding the phrase "of this [practitioner] who possesses the ten stages beginning with the *pīṭhas*," it means that for this practitioner, the *pīṭhas* and so forth—such as Pullīramalaya and the rest—are the very nature of the ten stages beginning with *muditā*. By all of this, it is established that all these things, beginning with one's mother, should be purified by contemplating them in the form of the perfections (*pāramitā*) and so on.

He asks how this can be made otherwise through meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) and says, "By whatever," and so forth. "By means of [cultivation]" (*bhāvena*) refers to the perfections (*pāramitā*) and so on. "Consisting of that" (*tanmayatām*) means having the nature of the perfections and so on. "Like a jewel of universal form" (*viśvarūpo maṇiḥ*): the meaning is that just as a crystal stone, being transparent, becomes blue, yellow, or other colors when in proximity to objects that are blue, yellow, and so forth, so too is this mind. Concluding, he says, "In this way," and so forth; "in this way" means by this sequence.

"In whatever way it has taken root" means wherever it has become active, such as in the perfections (*pāramitā*) and so forth. "In both the fearful and the fearless" implies "in any place. "In meditation" (*dhyāna*) refers to meditating upon those perfections and so forth until the limit of Buddhahood is reached. "Merely by being thought of" means through cultivation prior to attaining Buddhahood. "Accomplishing all activities" means that it accomplishes whatever is desired for oneself and others; this is the meaning of "that mind. For this very reason, he says: "It is attained," and so forth.

"In birth" (*janmasi*) means in a lifetime. "Bestowing the fruits of enjoyment and liberation" (*bhuktimuktiphalapradam*) is connected with the preceding [phrase], meaning that one attains Buddhahood or the state of a Bodhisattva, which is capable of granting the desired fruits to both oneself and others. "For cultivation," and so forth. "Someone something": false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*), however, has ignorance as its cause. "Of the wise" (*jñāninām*) means of those who seek thorough understanding. "By which," and so forth. "That very [birth] through thousands of millions of births" (*sā... janmakoṭisahasraṃ vai*) means even by means of thousands of millions of births.

"I have revealed this for the sake of his full comprehension, [saying] 'it has been impelled by my gnosis. The meaning is that whatever was to be known by a practitioner through thousands of millions of births—expressed here by the word 'swiftly'—has now been made manifest. Regarding the phrase 'established in the system of yogic conduct,' this refers to the third [empowerment]. And he says 'insentient, etc. because this, when cultivated, does not have insentient objects and so forth as its domain. 'Of one lacking means' (*kūpāyasya*) means of one devoid of skillful methods. 'Knowledge like that of a child' means knowledge such as that of an ordinary person."

"Among the wise" (*jñāninām*) means among those who seek thorough knowledge. "Of an immature being" (*aparipācitasattvasya*) is a genitive used in the sense of the locative (meaning "among"). "With the seven minds beginning with pride" (*mānādisaptacetasā*) refers to pride, excessive pride, and so forth. "The absorption into Śrī Heruka" (*śrīherukasamāveśam*) means the essential nature of Śrī Heruka. "Of the great-souled master" (*ācāryasya mahātmanaḥ*) refers to the teacher of noble intent. The word "having learned from the presence of" (*antikād viditvā*) is to be supplied as an ellipsis. He states the benefit with the words beginning "in the practice of movement" (*saṃcāra-*) and so forth. "In the ritual of movement" (*saṃcāravidhau*) means the procedure for movement. "Served according to the rules of the ritual" (*vidhānavidhisevitam*) means one should serve it according to the prescribed method.

"Those too" means he [the practitioner]. Regarding "of the praise of the Omniscient One," the ellipsis is "he attains the majesty of all the Omniscient Ones. Regarding "the entire three worlds," the particle *ca* (and) should be understood here. In the phrase "vision" (*darśana*) and so forth, the nominative case is used everywhere in the sense of the instrumental. The meaning is: "by means of the vision and so forth of that Blessed One. Regarding "the placement of the contrary deity," this refers to the one called Pracetas, who possesses great power at the limit [of practice], as stated in the *Vistara-tantra*.

"Breaking the inverted mantras" means that the inverted mantras are extracted by means of "hā svāhā" and so forth. "The secret of inverted meditation" means that the sequence of meditation is described in a disordered order. "The accomplisher of all essences" means that all of this is the accomplisher of the essence of all, namely the Śrī Saṃvara. "Common to all tantras" means that this Blessed One, because his form is unsurpassed, is common to all other tantras.

"Of those whose minds are not yet ripened" means that even those whose minds are not yet ripened will awaken gradually; thus, [the teaching] is common to them as well. Regarding the mantras for interrogation (*anuyoga*) and so forth, the phrase "likewise the revealer of the *samaya*" means that because they are included within the meditative absorptions (*samādhi*) such as *yoga* and *atiyoga* by virtue of being cultivated, he is the revealer of their essential nature. Furthermore, he states "it has been said," etc., because this is not an object for those lacking merit. "The consolation of the Tathāgatas" (*tāthāgatāśvāsa*): the Tathāgatas themselves are "Tāthāgatas"; the consolation belonging to them is "that [consolation]. In that [consolation], [the teaching resides].

The meaning is "for the sake of consolation. [One might ask: "If this is an object accessible only to those possessing merit, then what means will there be for those devoid of merit? In response, it is said by the Blessed One that immediately after unhappiness arose for the Tathāgatas, a sign of consolation for the Tathāgatas was spoken. To the question "What was spoken?", he says: "With a pure body," and so forth; this is easy to understand. Thus ends the eleventh exposition. 11.

Regarding the passage beginning with "therefore, it need not be protected" and ending with "not the fire-oblation," the meaning is clear. If one asks, "If things such as what is to be protected are useless, then what is to be realized? he says: "In brief," and so forth. "In brief" means by way of encompassing everything, starting with that which is to be protected. "The form of the assembly of mind" (*cittasamājarūpī*): "mind" refers to the non-dual *bodhicitta* consisting of great bliss (*mahāsukha*). That itself is the "assembly" (*samāja*), because all phenomena have the nature of a single flavor. The remainder of the sentence is "the Blessed One has that as his form. Regarding the passage beginning with "that which is to be grasped," and so forth:

[6] That Blessed One is to be grasped by means of both conceptual and non-conceptual cognition of consciousness and gnosis (*vijñāna-jñāna*). "Intent upon the Guru’s teaching" means for a disciple who is solely devoted to the Guru’s instruction, but not for those outside the path, such as the *śrāvakas* and others. "And far from the treatise" means that even those who know external treatises remain far removed. Now he states the nature of the teacher: "By means of the method," and so forth; "method" refers to the method of service (*śuśrūṣā*). "Of the yogins" means of the practitioner (*yogī*).

"Devoted to the service of the guru" means intent upon attending upon the guru. "Having understood the scripture of characteristics," that is, having learned the entire *tantra* from the presence of the guru by way of both its meaning and its text; "the instructor of the heroes" means he becomes the revealer of the hero, whose nature is the venerable *Saṃvara*. To the question of how he instructs, he says: "Instantly," and so forth. "One whose self is the yoga of the instantaneous form" means one who possesses the yoga of *Saṃvara* without depending on [external] weapons.

"Like a sudden form-seal" means that at the very same moment as oneself, the wise one [perceives it]; "suddenly in every respect" because at that very time the celestial palace (*kūṭāgāra*) and so forth are completed. "Suddenly one should utter the mantra" means the intention is that one should utter the mantra beginning with *oṃ āḥ hūṃ*. "But having embraced the secret eye and hand, the first is the pair (*dvandva*)"—here, the nominative case is used in the sense of the locative; thus, "the first" is connected with what follows as "successively."

The meaning is that among these *kriyā* and other tantras, there is no Bhagavān at all in each successive one. It is stated in the *Tāthāgatāśvāsa*: "Because the Bhagavān is not mentioned in the *kriyā* and other tantras, there arose for the Tathāgatas a lack of happiness due to their lack of full knowledge, as previously described. Therefore, the Bhagavān spoke this for the purpose of providing them with consolation. What was spoken? He says: "It has been pointed out right here. This means it has already been stated by us in this very exposition. Therefore, he says: "Let it be taken as a basis for happiness."

"The wood-worm is other than the straw"—for this very reason, any other system of ritual action and so forth is as devoid of essence as straw. Now, in order to manifest its majesty, he says: "That alone is the life-force of living beings. Because it has the nature of non-dual consciousness of great bliss (*mahāsukha*), it is the vital breath of the world. That alone is the supreme syllable (*paramākṣara*) because it is without beginning or end. "That alone is all-pervading" because no stable entity exists apart from it.

"Abiding in all bodies" means that even the mobile world possesses that very nature. "He alone is the knower of the Buddhas' wisdom" means that he alone is the wisdom of the Buddhas. "It is proclaimed as Śrī Heruka" means that he alone is called Śrī Heruka. "Because he maintains even the subtle aggregate" means that he alone is maintained by worldly beings in the form of both the subtle and the gross aggregates. "And all the treatises" refers to all the tantras; "the Vedas" refers to the external scriptures.

Regarding the term *siddhānta*: they are called *siddhāntas* because by means of them the end (*anta*) of rebirth is accomplished (*siddha*). They are the Śrāvaka-piṭaka and so forth. "Established" (*saṃsthitāḥ*) means that all these have arisen from that [source] and are established therein. Concluding, he says: "Consisting of the nature of the five Buddhas," and so on. "Consisting of the nature of the five Buddhas" refers to the essential form of the five Tathāgatas, Vairocana and the others. "This entire world" (*sarvajagaḥ*) refers to this entire world consisting of form, sensation, and so forth. "Of whom" (*yasya*) means "of which person" (*yaḥ punaḥ*).

"Sixth" refers to the sixth, known as Vajrasattva, whose alternative name is Mahāsukha. "By the name 'Buddha'" means that he is called by the name Buddha. "He dances alone with manifold flavors" means that he, though one, appears in manifold forms. He demonstrates this very multiplicity with the words beginning with "state" (*sthāna*). "State" means abiding; "and likewise through emergence" (*vyutthānataś caiva*) means emergence; "entry" (*praveśa*) means entering; "and likewise completion" (*niṣpattim eva ca*) means completion; and "empowerment" (*adhiṣṭhāna*) means empowerment.

"Samādhi" means meditative absorption (*samādhi*). "Upasaṃhṛta" means withdrawal (*upasaṃhṛti*). The intended meaning is that all this originates from great bliss (*mahāsukha*). "Vidhisaṃjñaṃ vai" means that which is a procedure (*vidhi*) by way of a designation (*saṃjñā*) is "designated as a procedure"; the sense is "by means of the procedure. "The non-duality of wisdom and means" (*prajñopāyasyādvayam*) refers to the blending of *Ā* and *LI*, whose intrinsic natures are wisdom and means. "Right there" means from the form of *Ā* and *LI*. "All have emerged" is because *Ā* and *LI* are the very nature of wisdom and means.

The "agents of creation and destruction" refers to the heroes (vīra) and others. He speaks of non-duality with the words beginning with "a ā. "This is she" refers to the Blessed Lady (Bhagavatī), because [the letter] *ā* is the form of the Blessed Lady. "O Lord God" refers to the Blessed Lord God Śrī Saṃvara, because [the letter] *kā* is his form. Regarding "and this is the supreme consecration" (*adhivāsana*), the meaning is that by the mere utterance of this, the consecration of the deities and so forth occurs. Regarding "origination," it means the accomplishment [of the deity] from this very [mantra], which consists of wisdom and method.

With the words "and also the mantra," he speaks of the benefits of the mantras, beginning with "He who this... and so forth; this is easy to understand. Regarding the phrase "the ornament of the god there," it is because [the deity] has the form of a garland of fifty severed heads. Regarding "the girdle, the abode of all," it is because, by way of a girdle, [it] stands encircling [all], and thus it is the abode (*ālaya*) of all practitioners. To conclude, he says: "One should wear this... and so forth. Regarding "the awakener of all phenomena" (*sarvadharmāvabodhaka*), it is called the awakener of all phenomena because all phenomena are awakened (*avabudhyante*) by means of it.

The meaning is that this is because the scriptures that bring about awakening consist of the nature of *āli* and *kāli*. He speaks of the *mahāyoga-samādhi* with the words beginning "āli-kāli" and so forth. Since it has been explained by the Gurus in the *Sādhana-ṭippaṇī*, everything is easy to understand. Thus ends the twelfth instruction. 12.

Now, regarding the passage beginning with "Furthermore," etc.: "The non-duality of the Hero and the Yoginī" means the state of being of one nature, the non-duality of the Hero (Vīra) Saṃvara together with the Yoginīs. How is there non-duality? He says: "Śrī Heruka," etc. "The ground of the syllables" means that Pullīramalaya is the ground (*bhūmi*) of the syllables such as *puṃ* and so forth; this is the intended meaning. Regarding "Pullīramalaya is the head": through the transformation of the syllable *puṃ*, the head should be understood as having the essential nature of Pullīramalaya.

In this way, other [forms] as well are to be understood through the transformation of their respective syllables into those specific forms; and the deities in the form of the channels (nāḍī) belonging to each of them are to be described in the *Saptadaśanirdeśa*. "Even while engaged in sexual union" means even while performing sexual intercourse. "Having placed [the mantras] here or there" means that, staying wherever one may be, one should meditate on the sounds such as *puṃ* and so forth in their proper locations. "Even the three worlds are not moved" means that, this being the case, one becomes unassailable even by Hariharaṇa and others.

In the phrase "of the *lakṣyābhidhāna-tantra*," the genitive case is used in the sense of the ablative (*pañcamī*). By "by that" is meant "by that cause," namely, by the cause of its great benefits; the sense is that what has already been stated is now being extracted. To address the question of why it is being extracted, he says: "of the *Khasamata-tantra* consisting of one hundred thousand [verses]"—that is, of the *Khasamata-tantra* of one hundred thousand [verses]. In that [tantra], the reality (*tattva*) was revealed; this is precisely what was stated. "The essence of the *piṇḍa*" means the essence in the form of a *piṇḍa*; the "essence of the *piṇḍa*" is the form of the venerable *Saṃvara*.

"By the summary (uddeśa), emanation (nirmāṇa) is taught" means that by the statement of the summary, that which consists of the emanation body (nirmāṇakāya) is explained. "By the detailed exposition (nirdeśa), the enjoyment body (sāṃbhogika) is considered" means that by the detailed exposition, that which consists of the enjoyment body (saṃbhogakāya) is explained. "The complete detailed exposition (pratinirdeśa) indeed shows nirvāṇa as reality" means that the complete detailed exposition is non-different from the dharma body (dharmakāya). [7] To state the three bodies in another manner, he says: "The three bodies," and so forth.

The phrase "characterized by the Dharma, Sambhoga, and Nirmāṇa [bodies]" means that the mind-wheel (*cittacakra*) and the others are, respectively, the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) and so forth. "Of the merit of the accumulation of gnosis" means that which is to be attained through the accumulations of merit and gnosis. "Resting upon the two truths" means that because its essence consists of the two truths, it serves as the foundation for the two truths. To show those who possess reverence for this, he says "Durmukha," and so forth. "Durmukha" means one who is wicked by way of his face (*mukhabhāvena*).

"Of the dull and mute" means those who are both mentally dull and speech-impaired. "Of those with deficient wisdom" means those lacking in discernment. "Those of wrong views" means those possessed of false views. "Mockers of external treatises" means those devoted to outside scriptures. "Even the path of the guru is a thorn" refers to those for whom the instruction of the guru is like a thorn; having rejected all such people—if it is explained to others [only] when there is fame or respect—the meaning is that only then will they have respect. Thus, having set aside all these [obstacles], if it is explained to others, then they will have respect.

"Divided and undivided," and so forth. "Divided" (*bhāga*) refers to the distinction between wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*). "Undivided" (*abhāga*) is the absence of differentiation within that division; it is by that very distinction [that the following is explained]. "Therein" (*tatra*) refers to the inquiry concerning non-duality. "The Goddess, the Sovereign to be worshipped": because the Yoginīs are preeminent there, first the Goddess, the Sovereign Vajravārāhī, is to be worshipped. "The deity of the command" (*ājñādaivata*): the Lord, the Blessed One, who is the master in granting the command, is to be worshipped. "Afterwards" connects with what follows.

"Born as a hero" (*vīraja*) means born in the form of a hero. "The purpose of all movement" (*samastasaṃcāra*) means the goal of all movement. "Crossing over cyclic existence" (*saṃsārottaraṇa*) means the one who delivers sentient beings from cyclic existence. "Lord" (*prabhu*) means the master even of the three realms. "The emanation of all Vedas" (*samastavedanirmāṇa*) means the creator of all the tantras and so forth. To the question, "Of what nature is that non-duality? he says: "The established conclusion" (*siddhānta*), and so on. "Established conclusion" (*siddhānta*) refers to the tenet (*samaya*) that must necessarily be cultivated by Buddhists. "That" (*tat*) refers to non-duality.

"By you" means by you [the author]. "By the Buddhists and non-Buddhists" refers to the Śrāvakas and others. He demonstrates the very difficulty of understanding through the passage beginning with "correct words and corrupt words. Regarding the subject of correct words (*śabda*) and corrupt words (*apaśabda*), that which is the convention (*saṃketa*) is itself the path because it brings about the attainment of the meaning. "In accordance with that" means by way of that [convention]. "The summarized meaning" (*piṇḍārtha*) refers to the meaning in its condensed form known as the *Śrīsaṃvara*. "Extracted" means explained. "Correctly" means without error. "The expansion of conventional terms" means by means of extensive, conventionalized words.

The meaning is that because it is expressed through both correct words (*śabda*) and corrupt words (*apaśabda*), it is difficult to understand. "He who does not know the movement" means he who does not know the purpose of the movement. "Yoga, yoga"—by saying "the yogi," he demonstrates his own state of being a yogi. "Of them" refers to him. "Its fruit" refers to the fruit of the purpose of the movement. Demonstrating the difficulty of understanding in another way, he says: "It has been said," and so forth. "Previously" means before. "By the primordial being" means by the primordial being [in the form of] the restraint (*saṃvara*).

"Spoken by another" means expressed by a word that is not [the primary] signifier. "A practitioner who is well-composed" means it should be understood by a practitioner whose mind is concentrated (*samāhita*) upon the objects of hearing and reflection; this is the meaning. Now he describes the power of the *āli* and *kāli* vowels and consonants, beginning with the words "It is said," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "whatever action one performs, whether auspicious or inauspicious, one should contemplate": the sense is that whatever auspicious or inauspicious thing the practitioner contemplates, all of that is accomplished for him.

"Situated in the midst of the other syllables" means being encircled by the vowels (*āli*) and consonants (*kāli*). "Therein" refers to that [enclosure]. "All are accomplished" means everything becomes perfected. Thus ends the thirteenth instruction. || 13 ||

"Then," and so forth. "In all tantras" means in the tantras of ritual action (*kriyā*) and the others. "Seated upon the thrones of the four Buddhas" means seated upon a sun-disc throne situated on the summit of Mount Sumeru, which rests within a square maṇḍala purified by the thrones of the four Buddhas marked with cow-dung and other substances, located in the space before oneself. "Vajra and so forth" refers to the primordial Vajrasattva, whose alternative name is Saṃvara. The word "should worship" is to be supplied. To the question "Of what nature [is he]?", he says: "The heroes and yoginīs," and so forth. "Heroes and yoginīs" refers to Vajravārāhī.

Regarding the phrase "the *ḍākinīs* and so forth": this refers to the wheel (*cakra*) consisting of the fourfold group beginning with the *ḍākinīs*. "The Lord, the Hero-Yogeśvarī" refers to the leader of the heroes (*vīra*) and yoginīs such as Khaṇḍakapāla who reside in the three wheels, as well as the eight [deities] beginning with Kākāsyā. "The four, the mirror and so forth" refers to the four skull-cups in the corners, filled with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) purified as the mirror, taste, touch, and phenomena (*dharma*). As for how one should worship, he says: "by means of the yoga of non-duality and duality. Here, "non-dual" refers to the Blessed One joined with Śrī Vajravārāhī.

Therefore, "non-dual union" (*advayayoga*) refers to the ego-identification with non-duality. The meaning is that, being oneself the leader of the mandala (*cakranāyaka*), one should worship the Blessed One. "Non-dual" means seeing the non-distinction between the object of worship, the worshipper, and the act of worship, by virtue of their being mind-only (*cittamātra*). "Substances, flowers, and so forth" refers to substances, as well as flowers, incense, and the like. He says this very thing with the words beginning with "should be given. "Flowers" refers to flowers and so on. "Each one" means individually; the meaning is that each [offering] should be given to the deities one by one.

Having thus described the external worship (*bāhyapūjā*), he speaks in order to demonstrate the hand-worship (*hastapūjā*): "With the five seals" (*pañcamudrā*) and so forth. "Of one whose body possesses the five seals and so forth" means by one who, preceded by the ego-identification (*ahaṃkāra*) with the glorious *Saṃvara*, wears the five seals upon the body; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the inclusion of ashes is intended. "By those who have gone to the further shore of the six perfections" means by one who has reached the further shore of the six perfections through the wearing of the seals, which are the embodiments of the perfections (*pāramitā*). "Hand-worship and so forth": hand-worship itself is the "beginning" because it is the primary [element].

"Of the knowers" means of Vajrasattva and others who are worthy of worship; "by the practitioner" means by one endowed with thorough knowledge. "It is to be known" means that which is to be understood. "The heroic and wise" means joined with the Heroine Vajrayoginī. The meaning is that the worship of the Heroines and Yoginīs is to be performed with the left hand. As for how many those deities are, he says: "six Yoginīs," meaning the six Yoginīs beginning with Vajravārāhī. "As before" means as they were described in their seed-syllable form during the section on the armor-mantra (*kavaca*).

"Vajrasattva and so forth" means Vajrasattva and the other five, making six. "Twelve" means those deities become twelve. Furthermore, the various other deities are to be understood from the Root Tantra (*mūlatantra*). "He who knows this" means he who, having known it. "The great hero" refers to the practitioner (*sādhaka*). "Mixed with five times five" means with flowers and so forth, accompanied by the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) and the five lamps (*pañcapradīpa*). "But mixed with Śrī Heruka" means, in the absence [of the aforementioned substances], with the mere *bodhicitta* (semen); such is the meaning. "Is to be worshipped" means he worships.

"Saṃsthāna" means in the correct position, namely, in the left hand. "Bhuktimuktiṃ tu kāmikam" means that his desired goal, characterized by enjoyment and liberation, comes to pass. "Daridram" means poor. "Hastapūjeneti" means by means of hand-worship. "Prāpyeti" means he attains. "Pūjābhir" refers to worship. "Eṣa vīro mahāvīra" means these heroes, such as Vajrasattva and others, are themselves Śrī Saṃvara. "Durlabham" means they are difficult to attain.

The phrase "the vow of conduct" (*caryāvrataṃ tu*) and so forth should be connected immediately after "this bestows the fruit of all desires. "This" refers to the hand-worship (*hastapūjā*) just mentioned. "One should worship oneself" means one should perform it personally. "Bestowing the fruit of all desires" means that the form of Śrī Saṃvara, which is capable of granting the fruits of all desired objects, is accomplished for him. "The vow of conduct" refers to the procedure of conduct (*caryāvidhi*) that is about to be described. The word "again" (*punaḥ*) should be supplied [after "obtaining"], as in "having again obtained. "Of the yoginīs" refers to the yogi.
"The Lord of all masters of yoga" means that he becomes the master of all other yogis; such is the meaning. This is the fourteenth instruction. 14.

[8] Now, regarding the passage beginning with “the procedure for conduct” (*caryāvidhi*) and so forth: “The hero” (*vīra*) refers to the practitioner whose nature is the vow (*saṃvara*). “The non-dual yoginī” means one who is joined in non-dual yoga with the *vidyā*; the meaning is that he possesses wisdom (*saprajña*). “Capable” (*śakta*) means possessing a slight power of yoga. “The practice of the vow” (*vratacaryā*) refers to the vow of conduct (*caryāvratam*). “As desired by the mind” (*manepsita*) means any one of the three types of conduct. “Great heroes” (*mahāvīrāḥ*) refers to practitioners. “Dwelling in garments made of animal limbs” means those who have donned a tiger skin as their lower garment.

"One seeking pleasure should move for the sake of pleasure" means that when they are seekers of the pleasure of sexual union (*surata*), they then produce pleasure. "The sacred thread," and so forth: the sense is that, having abandoned the sacred thread prescribed by the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*, their bodies are purified by other means of purification. "One should desire" means those who are desiring. "All yoginīs" refers to all the yoginīs associated with the five families (*pañcakula*). "If one should wish" means if such a desire arises.

"By those seeking the fruits of enjoyment and liberation" (*bhuktimuktiphalārthibhiḥ*) means those who desire the fruits of enjoyment and liberation. Now he explains the various forms of purification, such as that consisting of mantras and so forth, beginning with "of the root mantra" (*mūlamantrasya*). "Of the root mantra" (*mūlamantrasya*) refers to the *mālāmantra*. "Of whomsoever the hero" (*yadvīra*) refers to [the mantra] of whichever hero. "The sacred thread and so forth" (*brahmasūtrādī*) refers to the sacred thread established by tradition. "The garland indeed adorned with fifty" (*mālā vai śatārdhabhūṣitam*) refers to the garland of fifty severed heads. "With six of the armor" (*ṣaḍbhiḥ kavacasya*) refers to the six armor-mantras. "By the hero" (*vīreṇa*) refers to the hero.

"This mudrā is for the beautification of the limbs" refers to the six mudrās that adorn the body. "The mantra of Vajravārāhī" refers to the *mālā-mantra*. "A necklace upon the neck" refers to a necklace worn around the neck. "Beautiful" refers to Śobhanā. "By the *ḍākinī* of all Buddhas" refers to the heart mantra beginning with *oṃ sarvabuddhaḍākinīye*. "Wearing a garment of skin as supreme" means wearing a tiger-skin garment as one's supreme attire. "The form of the deity" refers to the body of Saṃvara.

"Conceived as the *ḍamaru* of wisdom" means that Vārāhī is the *ḍamaru*. "Conceived as the elements" means they are established in the form of nails, teeth, and so forth. "With the seven-syllable mantra" refers to the *upahṛdaya* (heart) mantra. "With the mantra of the six Yoginīs" refers to the six armor-mantras (*kavaca*) of the Yoginīs. "With the mantras of the Yoginīs of the entire wheel" refers to the mantras of the Yoginīs residing in the three wheels. "The skull-cup for drinking the mantra" is the vessel for the nectar of gnosis (*jñānāmṛta*). "Vairocanī" refers to the mantra.

The *upahṛdaya-mantra* of the Goddess. "Having thus contemplated oneself" means: having armored oneself (*kavacayitvā*) according to the sequence just described; one should perform continuous protection by repeatedly reciting the *ākṣepa-mantra*, which is the four-faced mantra. "Celibacy" (*brahmacarya*) refers to the practice (*carya*), that is, the conduct (*caraṇa*) of observing phenomena through the nature of restraint (*saṃvara*) which is Brahman. "Always being [thus]" means having done so continuously.

Regarding the phrase "one should indeed worship the mantra with the eightfold [formula]," one should worship oneself and others, such as the Guru and the Buddhas, by means of the eightfold mantra. The passage beginning with "the day," however, is easy to understand. Regarding "as with oneself" and so forth: "as with oneself" means that just as there is the notion of "I" (*ahaṃkāra*) toward oneself, so too toward sentient beings; and "so toward oneself" means that just as there is the notion of "I" toward others, so too toward oneself. "I am supreme" means "I am the highest"; this is the meaning of *saṃvara*.

"Abiding in the state of Śrī Heruka" means because they abide in the state of Śrī Heruka; this is the intended meaning regarding the "yogins. Regarding the phrase "five colors," and so forth: in reality, the universe is of but a single color, yet it is conceptualized as having five colors. Therefore, the meaning is that conduct within that [state] is not contradictory. He states the fruit of such conduct with the words beginning "these," and so forth: these beings who practice the conduct wander—that is, they go—to the "supreme state," which is the state of Śrī Saṃvara.
"With a mind of non-dual gnosis" means by means of the ego-identity (*ahaṃkāra*) of Śrī Saṃvara. Thus ends the fifteenth instruction. (15)

Regarding the passage beginning with "here, in the final time," etc.: "final" refers to the Kali age. "In this" means while there is a turmoil of afflictions (*kleśa*). "Is not accomplished" should be understood to refer to "people. "Thou" refers to you. "Think" means consider. To the question, "Is it not accomplished in every way? he says: "Except for that which is called 'Buddha'"; that is, apart from the *Śrī-saṃvara*, one designated as a Buddha is not accomplished—this is the sense that follows. "By the mudrā," etc., means even by means of the mudrās and so forth.

The connection with what follows is: "they do not at all attain accomplishment (*siddhi*). To the question "In what way? he says: "They go happily," and so forth. Just as those afflicted by hunger and thirst due to the power of disease go happily even after eating and drinking; the word "not at all" connects with what precedes—it means "in that same manner. "Desire" (*icchām*) means if there is a desire. "With effort" (*yatnena*) means with diligence. "I" (*aham*) refers to me. "In reality" (*tattvena*) means in its true form. "By the yogi" (*yoginā*) means by the practitioner of yoga.

"One who possesses the knowledge of Śrī Heruka" means one who knows the purification of Śrī Heruka as it truly is. "Wandering" means he roams. "As desired" refers to the *pīṭhas* and so forth. He states the fruit of wandering with the words beginning with "from afar. By the grace of the yoginīs, he hears sounds from afar as if they were nearby. "He sees with his eyes in an instant" means he sees even a form that is obstructed as if it were nearby. In this way, the other three superknowledges (*abhijñā*) are also to be understood.

"Having thus known these phenomena" means according to the sequence stated above; "having understood these benefits. Regarding the plural form "fulfilling all hopes," [it refers to the vows]. "The excellent vow of non-dual gnosis" means the vow of conduct that brings about non-dual gnosis. To demonstrate the non-duality of wisdom (*prajñā*) and skillful means (*upāya*) for the world, he says "Āli-kāli," and so forth. "Free from Āli and Kāli" means devoid of wisdom and skillful means that are not differentiated. "This phenomenon" refers to both the external and the internal.

"If he thinks" (*yadi manyakaḥ*) means if he thinks. The word "person" (*janaḥ*) is to be supplied [from the context]. It is easy to understand that his exertion is in vain and he will not obtain its fruit. Regarding the phrase "in the sūtras, etc. (*sūtrādiṣu*), the concise meaning is that this very same point has been set forth with the intention of benefiting others even in the sūtras and other scriptures. If one asks, "What, then, is the nature of wisdom and skillful means? he says: "But the engagement" (*pravṛttiṃ tu*) refers to the arising of the glorious *Saṃvara*. "As previously stated" (*yathā proktam*) means as it was explained before. "The two accumulations" (*sambhāradvayam*) means that which is to be attained through the two accumulations.

"Non-dual" means inseparable from primordial wisdom (*vidyā*). By this much, conventional truth has been explained. Desiring to speak of ultimate truth, he says: "He who knows the intrinsic nature of the reality of phenomena. Here, the nominative case is used in the sense of the genitive. "Reality" (*tattva*) is the brief designation; "phenomena" (*dharma*) is the explanation; and "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*) is the further specification. "By someone" refers to the syllable *Śrī*, which is non-dual gnosis, and so forth. Cessation is ultimate truth; thus it is stated. Concluding, he says:

It was said by me previously: "What was said? To this he replies: "Based upon the two truths. Here, the word "one should perform" (*kuryāt*) is to be supplied. "By the yogin" means by the practitioner. "The entire manifold of phenomena" (*sarvaprapañca*) refers to the forms of the gods and goddesses. "Having taken as an object" (*ālambya*) means one should take them as an object of focus. "As far as the sphere of cessation" (*nivṛtigocara*) means up to the limit of purification. In order to demonstrate that the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*) is common to all tantras, he says: "In all tantras," and so forth.

The meaning is that whatever secret *nirvāṇa* was shown in the *Kriyā* and other tantras, that too is shown here. Regarding the phrase "based upon the two truths," it should be understood that one should act [accordingly] even here. "Having cast aside all thoughts" means having abandoned all other thoughts. "He will move about" (*vicariṣyate*) means he moves about (*vicarati*). Regarding "the commitment of the Cakrasaṃvara," this refers to the sacred seats (*pīṭha*), secondary seats (*upapīṭha*), and so forth, within the enclosure of the Cakrasaṃvara. To the question "What having done?", he says: "Of this Yoginī," and so forth; "of this Yoginī" means of the Yoginīs.

"Having understood it to be a mere convention of form and a deceptive sign"—this is the ellipsis. "In a village of five houses, etc. means in villages and such places characterized by five houses. "They indeed abide" means they certainly remain there. "All [attainments] are accomplished for one who exists"—the meaning is that for this reason, he accomplishes all of them. "Intent on turning to the left" refers to the yogin who follows the left-hand path (*vāmācāra*). "Of the previously mentioned wheel"—here the genitive case is used in the sense of the accusative. "Having drawn" means having visualized. Now, he describes the process of becoming Heruka with the words beginning with "the mantra of the Hero," and so forth.

"Vīra-mantra-ādi-yoginīs" refers to the yoginīs beginning with Vīra. "One should perform the placement (nyāsa)" means one should perform the visualization (bhāvanā) in their respective locations. "The desired object of the mind" refers to the form of a donkey or other such forms as one wishes for in the mind. "Of the eastern petal" means on the petals starting from the east. "Ḍākinī" refers to Ḍākinī and the others. "Visualized in the form of a donkey" means they have been visualized in the form of a donkey. "By the name Śrīherukī, indeed, the transformation" means that this visualization is the transformation into Śrīherukī by means of that name.

"Performing all actions" means being engaged in every activity. "In body, speech, and mind" means by means of body, speech, and mind. "Whether spoken or unspoken" means either what has been said or what has not been said. "Contemplated" means resolved upon doing. "Abiding in the state of Śrī Heruka" means abiding in the yoga of the form of the venerable donkey-faced one (*gardabhākāra*). This is the sixteenth instruction. 16.

"From that," and so forth. "Of Śrī Heruka" refers to Śrī Heruka. "The sixth" refers to the sixth, Vajrasattva. "Mentally emanated" refers to that which has the nature of mind. "Of pure dharma" refers to emptiness (*śūnyatā*). "In that very [place]" means from those two bodies themselves. "By way of the union of the churner and the churned" refers to the perspective of meditating on the womb-born maṇḍala. "The four beginning with the mirror" refers to the four skull-cups, purified as the mirror and so forth, located in the corners.

"It is sung as 'the fourfold worship'" means that this very set of four worships is being described. "'Residing in the lotuses of the four ḍākinīs'" means the four ḍākinīs upon the four lotus petals. "'Māmakī and the others are the beautiful ones'" means that these very four ḍākinīs possess, as appropriate, the nature of Māmakī and the rest. "'Residing in the wheel'" means residing in the three wheels. "'Non-dual'" means absorbed in union with the Yoginī. "'Of the being who delivers from saṃsāra'" means of one who delivers sentient beings from cyclic existence.

"Beginning with Krodhavijayā and so forth" refers to Krodhavijayā and the others, such as Kākāsyā and the rest. "At the gates and corners" means at the gates and in the corners. "Up to the eighth" means until there are eight [deities]. He says "various," etc., in order to show that the death of a yogin is merely the resting of the mind. "By various means of discipline" means by various types of methods for disciplining sentient beings. "Diligent in performing the welfare of sentient beings": the nominative case is used in the sense of the genitive. "To be concealed" means it has been kept secret.

"Secret mantra" (*gūḍhamantra*) means that which is extremely esoteric. "Rest" (*viśrama*) means merely the resting of the mind. Here, one should connect it as follows: "The yogi rests the mind right here; nirvāṇa is not shown at all. "Yogi" (*yogī*) refers to practitioners of yoga. "Nirvāṇa" (*nirvāṇa*) refers to death. Regarding "the yoginīs and so forth," the phrase "up to the accomplishment cultivated by the hero" (*yāvat siddhibhāvitam*) means the cultivation of the yoginīs, heroes, and so on, up until their accomplishment. "Of those who have attained the fruit" (*phalaprāptasya*) means even those who have attained some degree of fruit. "Of the yogis" (*yoginām*) refers to the practitioners of yoga.

"In *saṃsāre*" means for those who wander in cyclic existence (*saṃsārin*). "For the sake of the welfare of disciples" (*hitāya śiṣyāṇām*) means for the benefit of disciples. The phrase beginning with "he who practices" (*yaḥ samācarati*) and so forth is easy to understand. In the expression "as before, etc., of evil" (*yathā pūrvādi pāpasya*), it is used in the sense of the instrumental case. "Of the yogins" (*yoginām*) refers to the yogis. Regarding "the heroes and yoginīs such as Śrī Heruka," the instrumental case is to be understood here and everywhere else as well. "The great hero god" (*devamahāvīra*) means the god who is the great hero. "The yoginīs" (*yoginyaḥ*) refers to the goddesses. "Difficult to obtain" (*durlabham*) means they are difficult to obtain.

"Just as women's talk and children's talk are approved"—meaning, just as joy arises for those possessed by passion through talk concerning women and men; and "talk of association and contact is proclaimed"—meaning, just as talk of the association and so forth between women and men is proclaimed for the sake of pleasure; "and the path is proclaimed, yet not bondage"—in the same way, the path and the absence of bondage are proclaimed [by whom?]. The word "by the Buddhas" is to be supplied.

"For one who knows thus, the path for the practitioner of yoga" means that for the practitioner who knows thus, the path is characterized by the union (*yoga*) of the God and Goddess. "The seats (*pīṭha*) and so forth are the abodes of the Yoginīs" means that the Yoginīs are said to reside in the places beginning with the *pīṭhas*. "The Heroes are established in non-duality" means they abide having attained the state of being one with the Hero (*vīra*). "Pullīra," and so forth, is easy to understand. "The Yoginī of the non-duality with the Hero" means she has attained the non-dual union with the Hero.

"Vāmasādhana" means for the sake of the practice (*sādhana*) of the *yoginīs*. "With the method" (*sopāyena*) means together with the method for the sake of propitiation (*ārādhanā*). "Having brought forth" (*uttārya*) means having crossed over. He states the sequence of meditation (*bhāvanākrama*) starting with "the necklace" (*kaṇṭhikā*) and so forth; this is easy to understand. "One should turn it" (*vartayet*) means one should rotate it. "By water" (*vāriṇā*) means by Akṣobhya. "By perfumes" (*gandhakaiḥ*) means by Vairocana. "The form of colors and so forth" (*varṇakācchādirūpam*) means one should produce the form of white and other colors by means of pigments (*varṇakaiḥ*). "Transformation by tone" (*svareṇa parivartanam*) means that "tone" (*svaraḥ*) is the speech of the wrathful deities, namely the syllable *hūṃ*.

Therefore, one should meditate on the accomplishment of the self. "For one engaged in the observance of conduct" means for one who maintains the elaborate conduct (*saprapañcacaryā*). "Well-established in yoga" means being correctly situated in yoga. "Sāttvika" refers to the dramatic sentiments (*nāṭyarasa*) such as the heroic (*vīra*) and the loathsome (*bībhatsa*). "Auspicious and great" means that once the drama has been performed, he becomes exceedingly dear to the *yoginīs*; this is the meaning. "Unpierced," etc., is the brief statement (*uddeśa*); "unpierced," etc., is the detailed explanation (*nirdeśa*).

"The thread should consist of a single strand" means that the *brahmasūtra* (sacred thread) should be made with a single string. "The girdle, however, consists of eight strands" means the girdle should be fashioned from eight strings. "The waistband is known to have sixteen [strands]"—the term *rasanā* refers to a specific type of girdle; it should be understood as being composed of sixteen strings. "But the garland has twenty-five" means the skull-garland (*muṇḍamālā*) should be made of twenty-five skulls; or alternatively, "garland" (*mālinam*) refers to a necklace.
And that should be understood as consisting of twenty-five pills. Thus ends the seventeenth exposition. 17.
Whatever merit I have acquired by clarifying the system of the movements that traverse the sky, resembling the moon,
may it be for the benefit of the entire world.
The attainment of perfect enlightenment will occur before long, without any suffering.
Thus ends the Saṃcāratantranibandha.
